notes.summary: English Composition in WBCS Prelims tests practical grammar and vocabulary: subject-verb agreement, tenses, articles, prepositions, voice, narration, error spotting, synonyms and antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms, spelling, sentence ordering and short comprehension passages. Each question has one clearly best answer, so knowing the rule behind it is faster than going by what sounds right.
keyPoints: Subject-verb agreement: with 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Neither the manager nor his assistants were...). 'Each', 'every' and 'one of' take a singular verb. 'The number of' takes a singular verb and 'a number of' a plural one.
Fixed pairs: hardly/scarcely...when, no sooner...than, both...and, not only...but also. A negative adverb at the start of a sentence inverts the verb (Hardly had I...).
Active to passive: keep the same tense. Has approved becomes has been approved, is writing becomes is being written, and will finish becomes will be finished.

Direct to indirect with a past reporting verb: am/is becomes was, will becomes would, can becomes could, and the present perfect becomes the past perfect. Now becomes then, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, and here becomes there. 'Said to' becomes 'told'.

Question tags: a positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement a positive tag, using the same auxiliary (She can swim, can't she? He never lies, does he?). 'I am' takes 'aren't I', and 'Let's' takes 'shall we'.

Spelling: when the stress falls on the last syllable, double the final consonant before a suffix starting with a vowel (occur → occurred, occurrence; begin → beginning). If the stress is earlier, do not double it (visit → visited). Watch accommodate (cc, mm), embarrass (rr, ss) and necessary (one c, double s).

Sentence ordering: the opening sentence has no pronoun or linking word. Each pronoun (it, these, this) and connector (also, however, therefore) must follow the sentence it refers to, and a summing-up sentence comes last.
Reading comprehension: an inference must be supported by the passage. Reject options that are extreme (only, always, never) or that contradict any line.

One-word substitution: plutocracy (rule by the wealthy), oligarchy (rule by a few), theocracy (rule by religious leaders), autocracy (rule by one person with absolute power), polyglot (speaks many languages), incorrigible (cannot be reformed).
traps: Making the verb agree with the first subject in a 'neither...nor' sentence.
Changing the tense in the passive (has approved → was approved) instead of keeping it.
Forgetting to change time words in indirect speech (tomorrow → the next day), or writing 'said me'.
Picking a word that only sounds similar: diligent and intelligent, accommodate and accumulate.
Marking 'Hardly...when' as an error because you are thinking of 'no sooner...than'. Each opener has its own partner word.
notes.examTip: In error spotting, find the subject and verb and check that they agree, then check tense and fixed pairs such as hardly...when. Choose 'No error' only after these checks pass, but do not shy away from it when they do.

questions.explanation:
The correct spelling has a double c, a double r and ends in -ence: o-c-c-u-r-r-e-n-c-e.
The stress in 'occur' falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles before a suffix that starts with a vowel (occurred, occurring, occurrence).
Answer: Occurrence.

questions.text: Choose the word most similar in meaning to 'DILIGENT'.
questions.explanation:
'Diligent' means showing steady care and effort in one's work.
'Lazy' and 'careless' are nearly its opposites.
'Intelligent' sounds similar but means clever, not hard-working.
Answer: Hard-working.

questions.text:
Choose the correct question tag:
'She can swim very well, ___?'
questions.explanation:
A positive statement takes a negative tag.
The tag repeats the auxiliary verb of the statement, which here is 'can'.
So the tag is 'can't she?'
Answer: can't she.

questions.text:
Choose the correct passive form of the sentence:
'The committee has approved the proposal.'
options: The proposal was approved by the committee.
The proposal had been approved by the committee.
The proposal is being approved by the committee.
The proposal has been approved by the committee.
questions.explanation:
The active sentence is in the present perfect (has + approved).
The present perfect passive is has/have + been + past participle.
The object 'the proposal' becomes the subject, and because it is singular it takes 'has been approved'.
The other options change the tense: 'was approved' is simple past, 'had been approved' past perfect, and 'is being approved' present continuous.
Answer: The proposal has been approved by the committee.

questions.text:
Choose the correct indirect form of the sentence:
He said to me, 'I am going to Delhi tomorrow.'
options: He told me that he was going to Delhi the next day.
He told me that he is going to Delhi tomorrow.
He said me that he was going to Delhi the next day.
He told me that I was going to Delhi the next day.
questions.explanation:
'Said to me' becomes 'told me'.
The reporting verb is in the past, so 'am going' becomes 'was going'.
'I' refers to the speaker, so it becomes 'he'.
'Tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.
'Said me' is ungrammatical, and 'I was going' changes who is travelling.
Answer: He told me that he was going to Delhi the next day.

questions.text:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Neither the manager nor / his assistants was / present at the meeting.
questions.explanation:
With 'neither...nor' and 'either...or', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
The nearer subject, 'his assistants', is plural, so the verb must be 'were', not 'was'.
Correct sentence: Neither the manager nor his assistants were present at the meeting.
Answer: his assistants was.

questions.text:
Sentence 1 is given. Arrange P, Q, R and S in the correct order to form a coherent paragraph.
1. The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world.
P. Its dense network of tidal rivers and creeks makes it difficult to explore.
Q. These tides also bring in salt water, which only special trees can tolerate.
R. Twice a day, the tides flood large parts of the forest floor.
S. This rich but harsh habitat is the home of the Royal Bengal tiger.
questions.explanation:
'Its' in P refers to the Sundarbans in sentence 1, so P comes next.
R introduces 'the tides', which follows from the 'tidal rivers' in P.
Q says 'These tides also...', so it must come after R.
S sums up the paragraph ('This rich but harsh habitat') and closes it.
Answer: PRQS.

questions.text:
Read the passage and answer the question.
Many villages in the delta once depended entirely on the monsoon for a single crop of rice. When small irrigation channels were dug from a nearby river, farmers began to grow a second crop in winter. Their incomes rose, but so did their use of chemical fertilisers, and within a decade some fields showed signs of declining fertility. Experts now advise a mix of organic manure and crop rotation.
Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: The gains from a second crop came with a long-term risk to soil health.
Irrigation brought only benefits to the villages.
Farmers stopped growing rice once irrigation arrived.
Experts want farmers to return to a single rain-fed crop.
questions.explanation:
The passage says incomes rose (a gain), but heavier fertiliser use led to declining fertility (a risk). That supports the first option.
'Only benefits' contradicts the declining fertility.
Nothing says farmers stopped growing rice; they added a second crop.
The experts advise organic manure and crop rotation, not a return to one crop.
Answer: The gains from a second crop came with a long-term risk to soil health.

questions.text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
'The new public library opened last week. Its spacious reading room, which can ___ nearly two hundred readers at a time, was full on the very first day.'
questions.explanation:
'Accommodate' means to have room for or to hold, so a room accommodates readers.
The other words do not fit: 'accumulate' means to gather over time, 'accompany' means to go along with, and 'acclimatise' means to adjust to a new climate or situation.
Answer: accommodate.

questions.text:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Hardly had I entered / the room when / the lights went out.
questions.explanation:
'Hardly' and 'scarcely' are followed by 'when', not 'than'. ('No sooner' is the one that takes 'than'.)
A negative adverb at the start of the sentence inverts the verb, so 'had I entered' is correct.
The past perfect (had entered) marks the earlier action and the simple past (went out) the later one.
The sentence is correct.
Answer: No error.

questions.text:
Choose the one word that best substitutes the phrase:
'Government by the wealthy'
questions.explanation:
Plutocracy comes from the Greek 'ploutos', meaning wealth: government by the rich.
The others: oligarchy is rule by a few people (not necessarily rich), theocracy is rule by religious leaders in the name of God, and bureaucracy is rule by officials.
Answer: Plutocracy.
